summary: Provides a framework for survivability in MPLS-TP networks, covering how traffic delivery recovers after failure or degradation of network resources. This is critical for services under strict service level agreements. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If a road is blocked, traffic should find a detour. This describes the plans MPLS-TP networks use to keep data moving when something breaks.

questions: what is the difference between protection and restoration
subtitle: The framework for keeping MPLS-TP traffic flowing after a link or node fails, through protection, restoration and OAM-driven switching.

tldr.problem: Transport networks that sell guaranteed services under SLAs must recover traffic quickly after a failure or degradation, and MPLS-TP may run with or without a control plane.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC organizes recovery by scope (span, segment, end-to-end), grade (dedicated, shared, extra traffic, restoration), topology (mesh linear protection, rings) and trigger (operator, OAM, control plane), all coordinated inside recovery domains.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework that reuses the recovery terminology of RFC 4427. It defines no protocol itself and leaves pseudowire recovery and ring mechanisms to other documents.

facts.label: Automated restoration
facts.value: Hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds

today: RFC 6372 is an Informational RFC published in September 2011, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a framework; the detailed protocols and ring and pseudowire mechanisms are specified elsewhere.

sections.title: Survivability in MPLS-TP
sections.content:
Network survivability is the ability to recover traffic delivery after a failure or degradation caused by a network fault or a denial-of-service attack. Services under Service Level Agreements (SLAs) need a network that detects failures very quickly and starts recovering at once. The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP, RFC 5921) aims to give operators protection and restoration that is similar to or better than established transport networks, and this framework meets the recovery requirements of RFC 5654 using the terminology of RFC 4427.

That terminology separates protection (re-establishing delivery with pre-allocated resources), restoration (using resources allocated at the time of need, usually by rerouting) and recovery (the generic term for both). The RFC says protection actions generally complete in tens of milliseconds, while automated restoration normally takes hundreds of milliseconds up to a few seconds, and is not guaranteed.

A distributed control plane is optional in MPLS-TP. Recovery can be triggered without one, by OAM or by management actions, and in every case the protection switch itself is a data-plane operation. Pseudowire recovery is outside the detailed scope: the RFC covers LSPs.
sections.eli5: Some customers are promised their data will keep flowing, so the network needs a quick backup plan. A spare road that is already built is fastest. Building a new road after the crash is slower and might not be possible.

sections.title: Scope, Grades and Reversion
sections.content:
Recovery scope says what is protected. Span recovery covers a single hop between neighbors (for example choosing another TE link from a bundle). Segment recovery covers one or more continuous hops of an LSP. End-to-end recovery covers the whole LSP and is a special case of segment recovery; it may be link-diverse or node-diverse, but the ingress and egress nodes remain single points of failure.

Grades of recovery trade speed against resources:

  • Dedicated protection: resources are pre-assigned to one protected path (1+1, or 1:1 without extra traffic).
  • Shared protection: recovery resources are shared, as 1:n or m:n. This saves capacity but risks leaving paths unprotected after a failure and adds delay from message exchanges.
  • Extra traffic: idle protection capacity carries preemptable traffic. Hard preemption excludes it completely; soft preemption gives it lower priority. RFC 5654 says support for extra traffic is not required in MPLS-TP.
  • Restoration: no resources are reserved, which uses the network most efficiently, but a new path must be computed and activated and success is not guaranteed.

Reversion returns traffic to the working LSP after repair. In revertive mode a configurable Wait-To-Restore (WTR) timer prevents flapping between paths when a defect is intermittent.
sections.eli5: You can keep a spare tire in the trunk (fast, but it takes space), share one spare among several cars (cheaper, but only one flat is covered), or call a tow truck (slowest, and maybe none is free).

sections.title: Recovery Domains and Protection Mechanisms
sections.content:
Recovery happens inside a recovery domain, bounded by reference end points at its edges. Recovery domains may be nested but must not overlap, and the edges of a domain are not protected unless another domain contains them. A recovery group holds a working entity and one or more recovery entities.

The RFC describes three kinds of protection mechanism:

  • Link-level protection, provided by a lower layer or the MPLS-TP link layer. It protects all LSPs on a link in one operation but does not protect the nodes at the ends.
  • Alternate paths and segments, where protection is done in the same layer as the LSP, end to end or for a segment.
  • Protection tunnels, pre-provisioned across a sequence of spans. Protected LSPs are switched into the tunnel at its ingress using label stacking.

In layered networks, recovery in several layers must be coordinated to avoid races. A configurable hold-off timer delays the MPLS-TP layer so a lower layer can fix the problem first. Links can inherit protection from the server layer, working and protection paths must not share a risk (for example two lambdas in one fiber, or two nodes in one building with a shared power supply), and fault correlation works out which single event caused many fault reports.
sections.eli5: A recovery domain is a stretch of road with a bypass built next to it. Both ends of the stretch need to agree on when to use the bypass, and the bypass must not run through the same flooded valley.

sections.title: Linear Protection in Mesh Networks
sections.content:
Linear protection works between any pair of points in a mesh and gives a clear indication of protection status. It runs inside a protection domain with a protection group of working and protection paths that should be physically diverse.

  • 1:1 and 1:n: traffic normally uses the working entity while the protection entity is idle. After a defect traffic is switched, and the source and sink must coordinate so bridging and selection use the same entity. With 1:n, one protection entity covers n working entities, and revertive behavior is recommended.
  • 1+1: traffic is copied to both entities and the sink selects between them. Unidirectional 1+1 needs no state coordination; bidirectional 1+1 does.
  • P2MP: 1+1 can protect a unidirectional point-to-multipoint LSP, where different leaves may select different entities. The RFC says mechanisms for other P2MP cases do not yet exist.
  • Shared mesh protection: protection resources are shared by LSPs that do not have the same end points. It is normally pre-planned by the operator.

Switching can be triggered by a defect found by OAM, an indication from a lower layer, an operator command such as Forced Switch or Manual Switch, or a request from the far end. For protection switching it is common to run a CC-V every 3.33 ms, and three missed messages declare a fault. For 50-ms protection switching the RFC recommends an in-band, data-plane signaling protocol to coordinate the two ends. To protect LSP segments, linear protection uses a Sub-Path Maintenance Element (SPME) over the Generic Associated Channel. Ring protection is only introduced, with its mechanisms specified in separate documents.
sections.eli5: In 1+1 you send two copies of the message down two roads and the receiver picks the better one. In 1:1 you use one road and keep the other empty for emergencies, and both ends have to agree when to switch.

sections.title: Management, OAM and Control Plane Mechanisms
sections.content:
Section 6 explains how recovery is configured, triggered and coordinated by three means.

The management plane sets the recovery domain end points, the working and recovery entities, the protection type, revertive behavior, and timers such as WTR and hold-off. Manual commands apply to a protection group, in descending order of priority: blocked protection, force protection, manual protection and clear switching.

OAM is the main way to detect faults in the MPLS-TP layer: proactive continuity checks and connectivity verification, signal degradation measurement, and remote defect indication. On-demand tools such as trace-route and loopback localize a fault, and a lock operation allows out-of-service testing. The protocol to coordinate protection state (specified in a separate document) also detects configuration mismatches between the two ends. Without coordination, protection switching fails.

The control plane is the GMPLS control plane, proposed for MPLS-TP. It cannot detect data-plane faults, so using it as the primary fault detection mechanism is not recommended, and routing-based fault indication is not considered fast enough to trigger protection switching. GMPLS does help with link testing (LMP), fault status reporting (the Notify message) and establishing protection and restoration LSPs (RFC 4872, RFC 4873, RFC 4874). All mandatory MPLS-TP survivability features must work even without a control plane.
sections.eli5: A recovery can be started by a person pushing a button, by an alarm that notices the break, or by the network's own messaging. The alarm is the fastest, and everything must still work if the messaging system is missing.

sections.title: Pseudowires, Manageability and Security
sections.content:
Pseudowires (PWs) can be protected by protecting the LSPs that carry them, or in the PW layer itself, for example by running separate PWs end to end. A single LSP recovery cannot protect a multi-segment PW against failure of a switching point (S-PE). Detailed PW recovery is left to a separate document.

The framework says it introduces no new security considerations. It notes that an attacker able to force a protection switch could perturb user traffic, displace extra traffic, or leave other traffic unprotected in 1:n or shared mesh protection. OAM messages for fault notification therefore need adequate security against bogus or replayed messages, manual command channels must support authorization, and control-plane protocols used for recovery must be secured too.
sections.eli5: If a bad actor could trick the network into switching roads for no reason, traffic would be disturbed. So the alarm messages and the buttons both need locks.

cells: Saves capacity; risk of unprotected paths, delay from coordination
Efficient but slower, and not guaranteed

items.label: Blocked protection
items.desc: Prevents traffic from switching to the recovery entity; disables the protection group.

items.label: Force protection
items.desc: Forces normal traffic onto the recovery entity.

items.label: Manual protection
items.desc: Switches traffic only when there is no defect in the recovery entity.

items.label: Clear switching
items.desc: Clears a previous manual or force switch.
